stem: Nationalism is best described as:
options: A sense of collective identity and belonging among a group of people who see themselves as a nation, and their aspiration to have their own political recognition or state
solution: Nationalism is a sense of collective political identity and belonging among a group of people who see themselves as forming a nation — sharing a common identity, history, and aspirations — and their aspiration to political recognition and self-determination, often in the form of their own state. It has been one of the most powerful political forces of the modern world.

stem: A 'nation' is different from other social groups (like families or tribes) mainly because it is:
options: A large community of people who may never meet, but who imagine themselves as belonging together on the basis of shared identity, aspirations, and a vision of a common political future
solution: A nation is different from smaller social groups because it is a large community of people, most of whom will never meet or know each other personally, but who nonetheless imagine and believe themselves to belong together as a single community — on the basis of a shared identity, common history and memories, shared aspirations, and a vision of a common political future. It is, in this sense, an 'imagined community' held together by a shared sense of belonging and collective identity.

stem: The idea that a nation is an 'imagined community' (associated with Benedict Anderson) means that:
options: The members of a nation imagine themselves as belonging to one community, even though they cannot all know one another personally
Nations are based on imagination alone with no consequences
solution: The idea that a nation is an 'imagined community' (associated with Benedict Anderson) means that the members of a nation imagine and conceive of themselves as belonging together as one community, sharing a common identity and bond, even though they cannot possibly all know one another personally (given the large size of nations). The nation is 'imagined' in the sense that it exists in the shared consciousness, sense of belonging, and collective imagination of its members — though this does not make it any less real or powerful in its effects.

stem: Which of the following is often cited as a basis of national identity, though no single one is essential to defining a nation?
options: Shared beliefs, common history, shared territory, common political ideals and aspirations, and sometimes a shared language or culture
Only the size of the army
solution: Various factors are often cited as bases of national identity — such as shared beliefs and a sense of belonging, a common history and shared memories, attachment to a common territory or homeland, shared political ideals and aspirations, and sometimes a shared language, culture, or ethnicity. However, no single one of these is essential to, or sufficient for, defining a nation; nations are formed on different bases, and what is most fundamental is the shared sense of collective identity, belonging, and common political aspiration among the members.

stem: A shared 'common history' contributes to national identity because:
options: A sense of a shared past, common memories, heroes, struggles, and achievements gives members of a nation a sense of collective identity and continuity
solution: A shared common history contributes to national identity because a sense of a shared past — common memories, experiences, heroes, struggles, triumphs, and even collective suffering and sacrifice — gives the members of a nation a sense of collective identity, belonging, and continuity, binding them together as a community with a shared heritage and story. The way a nation remembers and tells its history shapes its sense of who it is; a shared history helps create the 'we' feeling that is central to nationhood.

stem: Attachment to a particular territory (a homeland) is important to nations because:
options: People who see themselves as a nation usually have a strong sense of belonging to a specific territory or homeland, which is central to their identity and their aspiration for self-government there
Only the size of territory matters
solution: Attachment to a particular territory (a homeland) is important to nations because people who see themselves as a nation usually share a strong sense of belonging to, and identification with, a specific territory or homeland — a piece of the earth that they regard as their own, that is bound up with their history, memories, and identity, and over which they aspire to exercise self-government. The claim to a homeland is often central to national identity and to nationalist aspirations for self-determination and statehood.

stem: The principle of 'self-determination' claims that:
options: A people who see themselves as a nation have the right to determine their own political future and to govern themselves, ideally within their own state
Nations should never have their own governments
Foreign powers should decide a nation's future
solution: The principle of 'self-determination' claims that a people who regard themselves as a nation have the right to determine their own political destiny and to govern themselves — to be free from external (foreign) domination and, ideally, to have their own independent state or an appropriate degree of self-government. The principle of national self-determination has been a powerful and influential idea, inspiring nationalist and anti-colonial movements around the world in their struggles for independence and self-rule.

stem: The principle of self-determination played a major role in:
options: Anti-colonial national liberation movements (like India's freedom struggle), in which colonised peoples asserted their right to freedom and self-government
solution: The principle of self-determination played a major role in the anti-colonial national liberation movements of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries — including India's own freedom struggle — in which colonised peoples asserted their right, as nations, to freedom from foreign (colonial) rule and to self-government and independence. Nationalism and the demand for self-determination were powerful driving forces behind the struggles that led to the end of colonial empires and the emergence of many new independent nation-states.

stem: A serious problem or challenge posed by the principle of self-determination is that:
options: It is always easy to apply

It is very difficult to satisfy every group's demand for a separate state, since populations are often mixed and there are many groups claiming to be nations, so applying it fully could lead to endless fragmentation and conflict
solution: A serious challenge posed by the principle of self-determination is that it is very difficult, and often impossible, to satisfy every group's demand for a separate state of its own. Populations are usually mixed, with different groups living intermingled in the same territories, and there are far more groups claiming to be distinct nations than there could possibly be separate states. If every group claiming to be a nation were granted its own separate state, the result could be endless fragmentation, the creation of countless tiny and unviable states, the displacement of minorities, and much conflict and instability. This makes the full application of the principle deeply problematic.

stem: The existence of national, ethnic, or religious minorities within states means that:
options: Most states contain a mix of different groups, so the ideal of a state whose boundaries coincide exactly with a single, homogeneous nation is rarely, if ever, fully realised
solution: The existence of national, ethnic, linguistic, and religious minorities within states means that most states are not homogeneous but contain a mix of different groups and communities. As a result, the nationalist ideal of a 'nation-state' — a state whose boundaries coincide exactly with a single, homogeneous nation, in which one nation has its own exclusive state — is rarely, if ever, fully realised in practice; almost all states are, in fact, multinational or multicultural to some degree, containing diverse groups and minorities. This reality poses important challenges for nationalism and for the accommodation of diversity within states.

stem: When a state contains diverse groups, a key challenge is to:
options: Accommodate and respect the diversity of groups and the rights of minorities, while maintaining national unity — reconciling diversity with unity
solution: When a state contains diverse national, ethnic, linguistic, or religious groups (as most states do), a key challenge is to accommodate and respect the diversity of these groups and the rights of minorities, while at the same time maintaining the unity, integrity, and shared identity of the state and nation — that is, to reconcile diversity with unity. This involves finding ways to protect the rights, identities, and cultures of diverse groups and minorities, and to give them a sense of belonging and a fair place within the nation, without fragmenting the state or undermining national unity. How to combine unity with diversity — to hold a diverse society together while respecting and accommodating its diversity — is one of the central challenges for states and for nationalism in the modern world.

stem: Indian nationalism, as it developed during the freedom struggle, is often described as an example of:
options: A narrow nationalism based on a single religion or language
An inclusive nationalism that sought to unite people of diverse religions, languages, and regions in a shared struggle and a common national identity
A nationalism that excluded most Indians
A nationalism based on hatred of others
solution: Indian nationalism, as it developed during the freedom struggle, is often described as an example of an inclusive nationalism — one that sought to unite people of diverse religions, languages, cultures, regions, and communities in a shared struggle for freedom and a common national identity, rather than defining the nation narrowly on the basis of a single religion, language, or ethnicity. Indian nationalism embraced the country's diversity and sought to forge a sense of common nationhood and shared aspiration among its diverse peoples — an inclusive, composite, and pluralistic conception of the nation, reflected in the vision of 'unity in diversity'.

stem: Nationalism has had both positive and negative faces in history. A positive aspect of nationalism is that it:
options: Has inspired people to unite, to struggle for freedom from oppression and colonial rule, and to build a sense of common identity and solidarity
solution: Nationalism has had a positive face in history: it has inspired people to unite and to develop a sense of common identity, belonging, and solidarity; it has been a powerful force in the struggles of peoples for freedom from oppression, foreign domination, and colonial rule (as in the national liberation movements); and it has helped to build nations, foster a sense of shared purpose and community, and mobilise people for collective goals and the common good. In these ways, nationalism has been a force for freedom, unity, self-government, and collective identity and solidarity.

stem: A negative or dangerous face of nationalism is when it:
options: Becomes narrow, aggressive, or exclusive — breeding hatred and hostility towards other nations or towards minorities within, and leading to conflict, war, oppression, or the persecution of minorities
solution: Nationalism also has a negative and dangerous face: when it becomes narrow, aggressive, exclusive, or chauvinistic, it can breed hatred, intolerance, and hostility towards other nations or towards minorities within the nation. Such nationalism can lead to conflict, war, and aggression between nations; to the oppression, persecution, exclusion, or 'ethnic cleansing' of minorities who do not fit the dominant national identity; and to the suppression of diversity and dissent in the name of national unity. History provides many tragic examples of the destructive consequences of narrow, aggressive, and exclusive nationalism — reminding us that nationalism, though it can be a force for freedom and unity, can also be a source of great conflict, hatred, and injustice.

stem: The challenge for a nation is to develop a form of nationalism that:
options: Is inclusive and tolerant — fostering unity and common identity while respecting diversity, protecting the rights of minorities, and avoiding hatred of others
solution: The challenge for a nation is to develop a form of nationalism that is inclusive, tolerant, and civic — one that fosters a sense of unity, common identity, and solidarity among the members of the nation, while at the same time respecting and accommodating the diversity of groups within the nation, protecting the rights and identities of minorities, and avoiding narrow exclusiveness, chauvinism, and hatred of other nations or of minorities. Such an inclusive and tolerant nationalism seeks to combine unity with diversity, and national pride and solidarity with respect for the rights and dignity of all groups and with a peaceful and respectful attitude towards other nations — avoiding the dangers of the narrow, aggressive, and exclusive nationalism that breeds conflict, oppression, and hatred.

stem: The relationship between nationalism and democracy is that:
options: Nationalism can be connected to democracy through the ideas of popular sovereignty and self-determination — that the nation (the people) should govern itself — though nationalism can also take undemocratic forms
Nationalism has no relation to democracy
Democracy requires the rejection of nationhood
solution: The relationship between nationalism and democracy is complex. Nationalism can be closely connected to democracy through the ideas of popular sovereignty and self-determination — the idea that the nation (understood as the people) should be sovereign and should govern itself, free from external domination and from the arbitrary rule of a few. In this sense, nationalism and democracy grew up together historically and share the idea that the people/nation should rule themselves. However, nationalism can also take undemocratic and illiberal forms — when it becomes narrow, aggressive, or exclusive, suppresses dissent and minorities, or is used to justify authoritarian rule in the name of the nation. So while nationalism and democracy can be connected (through self-government and popular sovereignty), nationalism does not always go together with democracy, and can sometimes undermine it.

stem: The idea of a 'nation-state' refers to:
options: A state that claims to be the political expression and homeland of a particular nation — the ideal of one nation having its own state
A state ruled by many nations equally
solution: The idea of a 'nation-state' refers to a state that claims to be the political expression, embodiment, and homeland of a particular nation — the modern ideal in which each nation has, or aspires to have, its own state, and the boundaries of the state coincide with those of the nation. The nation-state has been the dominant form of political organisation in the modern world, and the aspiration of nations to have their own nation-states (national self-determination) has been a powerful force. However, as noted, the ideal of a homogeneous nation-state (one nation, one state) is rarely fully realised, since most states are in fact diverse and contain minorities.

stem: Nationalism became a powerful force in the modern world especially from which period?
options: The late 18th and 19th centuries (associated with events like the French Revolution and the rise of modern nation-states)
solution: Nationalism became a powerful political force in the modern world especially from the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, associated with events like the French Revolution (which promoted the idea of the nation and popular sovereignty) and the subsequent rise of modern nation-states, national movements, and struggles for national unification and independence across Europe and, later, the world (including the anti-colonial movements of the twentieth century). While a sense of collective identity is old, nationalism as a powerful modern political ideology and force — with its ideas of the nation, national self-determination, and the nation-state — is largely a product of the modern era.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Nationalism' is that:
options: Nationalism is always good or always bad

Nationalism is a powerful modern force that binds people into nations and has inspired struggles for freedom and self-government, but it can be either inclusive and tolerant or narrow and aggressive; the challenge is to build an inclusive nationalism that combines unity with respect for diversity and the rights of minorities
solution: The chapter concludes that nationalism is one of the most powerful political forces of the modern world: it binds people into nations — imagined communities sharing a collective identity, history, territory, and aspirations — and it has inspired great struggles for freedom, self-determination, and self-government (as in the anti-colonial movements), and helped build nations and foster unity and solidarity. However, nationalism has both a positive face (uniting people, inspiring freedom struggles, building solidarity) and a negative, dangerous face (breeding narrow, aggressive, or exclusive attitudes, hatred and hostility towards others and towards minorities, and leading to conflict, oppression, and persecution). The principle of self-determination, though powerful, cannot be fully applied to satisfy every group's demand for a separate state, since populations are mixed and states are diverse. The key challenge, therefore, is to develop an inclusive, tolerant, and civic form of nationalism — one that fosters unity, common identity, and solidarity while respecting and accommodating diversity, protecting the rights of minorities, and avoiding narrow exclusiveness and hatred — so as to reconcile national unity with the accommodation of diversity, as Indian nationalism at its best has sought to do. Nationalism, in short, can be a force for either freedom and unity or hatred and conflict, and the task is to cultivate its inclusive and positive form while guarding against its narrow and destructive one.

stem: Which of the following best captures the ideal of 'unity in diversity' as applied to a nation?
options: Achieving unity by eliminating all differences
Achieving and maintaining national unity while respecting, accommodating, and celebrating the diverse identities, cultures, languages, and communities within the nation
solution: The ideal of 'unity in diversity' captures the vision of achieving and maintaining national unity while at the same time respecting, accommodating, and even celebrating the diverse identities, cultures, languages, religions, and communities within the nation — building a unity that embraces and is enriched by diversity, rather than one that requires the elimination or suppression of differences. It holds that a nation can be genuinely united precisely by respecting and accommodating its diversity — giving all its diverse groups a fair place, recognition, and sense of belonging within an inclusive, composite nationhood — rather than by imposing uniformity or suppressing diversity. 'Unity in diversity' is a central ideal of Indian nationhood and of inclusive, pluralistic nationalism, expressing the aspiration to combine national unity with the respect and accommodation of diversity, and reflecting the conviction that diversity, far from being a threat to unity, can be a source of strength and the basis of a genuine and durable unity. It stands in contrast both to narrow, uniformity-imposing nationalism (which seeks unity through the suppression of diversity) and to fragmentation (which sacrifices unity), offering instead a vision of a united nation that embraces, respects, and celebrates its diversity.

stem: The 'right to self-determination' in international discussions has generally been understood, in practice, to apply most clearly to:
options: Every group that claims to be a nation, without limit
Colonised peoples seeking freedom from foreign rule, while its application to groups within existing states is far more contested
solution: The 'right to self-determination' in international discussions has generally been understood and applied most clearly and widely in the context of colonised peoples seeking freedom and independence from foreign (colonial) rule — where it provided a powerful and widely accepted basis for the decolonisation and independence of colonised peoples in the twentieth century. Its application to groups WITHIN existing (independent) states — that is, the claim of national or ethnic minorities within a state to secede and form their own separate state — is, by contrast, far more contested, difficult, and limited, because of the serious problems (of fragmentation, conflict, mixed populations, and new minorities) that such application would raise, and because of the general concern of existing states to preserve their unity and territorial integrity. Thus, while the principle of self-determination has been widely accepted and applied in the context of decolonisation (freedom from foreign rule), its application to groups within existing states (as a right to secede) is much more contested and limited, and is generally not accepted as an unlimited right of every group claiming to be a nation. This distinction — between the widely accepted application of self-determination to colonised peoples seeking freedom from foreign rule, and its far more contested application to groups within existing states — is an important one for understanding the scope, application, and limits of the principle of self-determination in international politics and practice.

stem: The recognition and celebration of a nation's diversity (rather than the imposition of uniformity) is characteristic of which kind of nationalism?
solution: The recognition, respect, and celebration of a nation's diversity — rather than the imposition of a single, uniform identity — is characteristic of an inclusive, pluralistic, and civic form of nationalism. Inclusive and civic nationalism understands the nation as embracing and being enriched by its diversity (of religions, languages, cultures, and communities), and defines national membership by shared political values and belonging that are open to all, rather than by a single ethnicity, religion, or culture; it therefore respects, accommodates, and even celebrates the nation's diversity, and seeks to unite its diverse peoples in an inclusive, composite nationhood ('unity in diversity'). This stands in contrast to narrow, exclusive, chauvinistic, or racist forms of nationalism, which define the nation narrowly (by a single ethnicity, religion, or culture), tend to impose uniformity and to suppress or exclude diversity and minorities, and can breed intolerance, exclusion, and hatred. The recognition and celebration of diversity — the inclusive, pluralistic embrace of the nation's diverse peoples and traditions — is thus a hallmark of the inclusive, civic, and pluralistic form of nationalism (exemplified at its best by Indian nationalism and its ideal of 'unity in diversity'), and it distinguishes this positive and inclusive form of nationalism from the narrow, exclusive, and uniformity-imposing forms that suppress diversity and exclude those who do not fit a single national mould.

stem: The distinction between 'nation' and 'state' is that a state is:
options: A political and legal entity with a defined territory, government, population, and sovereignty, whereas a nation is a community of people bound by a shared sense of identity and belonging
A community bound only by culture
solution: The distinction between 'nation' and 'state' is important. A state is a political and legal entity, defined by four elements: a defined territory, a population, a government, and sovereignty (supreme authority). A nation, by contrast, is a community of people bound together by a shared sense of collective identity, belonging, common history, and aspirations. The two do not always coincide: a state may contain more than one nation (a multinational state), and a nation may lack a state of its own (a stateless nation). The nationalist ideal of the 'nation-state' — where the nation and the state coincide — is often not fully realised in practice.

stem: The great Indian poet who was critical of narrow and aggressive nationalism, warning against its dangers while valuing love of one's country, was:
solution: The great Indian poet, writer, and thinker Rabindranath Tagore was critical of narrow, aggressive, and chauvinistic nationalism, warning against its dangers — its tendency towards hatred, aggression, and the worship of the nation at the expense of humanity and moral values. While Tagore loved his country and cared deeply for its freedom and well-being, he was wary of a nationalism that became narrow, exclusive, aggressive, or that placed the nation above humanity and moral values, and he emphasised the importance of universal human values, humanism, and a broad, humane, and inclusive outlook over a narrow and aggressive nationalism. His thoughtful critique of narrow nationalism, and his emphasis on humanity and universal values, represent an important perspective on the dangers of nationalism and the importance of a humane and inclusive outlook.

stem: 'Patriotism' is sometimes distinguished from 'nationalism' in that patriotism refers to:
options: A love of and devotion to one's country and its people, which can be inclusive and compatible with respect for others, as distinct from narrow or aggressive forms of nationalism
solution: 'Patriotism' is sometimes distinguished from 'nationalism' in that patriotism refers to a love of, devotion to, and pride in one's own country and its people — an attachment that can be inclusive, tolerant, and compatible with respect for other countries and peoples and with universal moral values. Nationalism, especially in its narrow or aggressive forms, by contrast, can involve an exclusive, chauvinistic, or aggressive attitude — a belief in the superiority of one's own nation and hostility towards others. On this distinction, patriotism (a positive, inclusive love of one's country) can be contrasted with narrow or aggressive nationalism (an exclusive, chauvinistic, or hostile attitude). The distinction highlights that love of and attachment to one's country need not take a narrow, exclusive, or aggressive form, and that it is possible — and desirable — to love one's country while also respecting others and upholding universal human values.

stem: 'Chauvinism' (or jingoism) refers to:
options: A balanced love of one's country
An extreme, aggressive, and unreasoning form of nationalism, marked by a belief in the superiority of one's own nation and hostility or contempt towards others
solution: 'Chauvinism' (and the related term 'jingoism') refers to an extreme, aggressive, blind, and unreasoning form of nationalism — marked by an exaggerated and uncritical belief in the greatness and superiority of one's own nation, and by hostility, contempt, or aggression towards other nations and peoples. Chauvinistic nationalism is the negative, dangerous face of nationalism: it fosters hatred, intolerance, and aggression, glorifies the nation uncritically, and can lead to conflict, war, and the oppression of others and of minorities. It is contrasted with a healthy, balanced, inclusive, and tolerant love of and attachment to one's country. Chauvinism and jingoism represent the excessive and dangerous forms of nationalism that history warns us against.

stem: The right of a national group to break away and form its own separate state is called:
solution: The right or act of a national group (or a region) to break away and separate from an existing state in order to form its own separate independent state, or to join another state, is called 'secession'. Demands for secession — for a group to break away and form its own state — often arise from strong nationalist or separatist sentiments among a group that feels it constitutes a distinct nation and wishes to have its own state. Secession is a highly contentious and difficult issue: while it may be claimed as an expression of the right of self-determination, it is often resisted by the existing state (which seeks to preserve its unity and integrity), and it can lead to conflict, instability, and the problem of new minorities within the seceding territory. The question of when, if ever, secession is justified is a difficult and contested one, connected to the challenges of applying the principle of self-determination.

stem: The idea that nations are 'modern' constructions rather than ancient, natural entities is associated with which view of nationalism?
options: That nations have always existed unchanged
The 'modernist' view (associated with thinkers like Ernest Gellner and Benedict Anderson), which holds that nations and nationalism are products of modern conditions and processes
solution: The idea that nations are 'modern' constructions rather than ancient, natural, or eternal entities is associated with the 'modernist' view of nationalism, held by thinkers like Ernest Gellner and Benedict Anderson. On this view, nations and nationalism are not ancient or natural, but are relatively modern phenomena — products of specifically modern conditions, processes, and developments (such as the rise of the modern state, industrialisation, the spread of print, mass education, and modern communication). Rather than nations giving rise to nationalism, it is argued, nationalism (and modern conditions) gave rise to nations — nations were, in a sense, 'constructed' or 'imagined' under modern conditions. This modernist view — that nations and nationalism are modern constructions rather than ancient, natural givens — is an influential perspective in the study of nationalism, though it is debated by those who emphasise the older roots of national identities.

stem: The spread of 'print' and a common written language is said (by Benedict Anderson) to have helped create nations because it:
options: Enabled large numbers of people who would never meet to share a common language, ideas, and sense of belonging, helping them imagine themselves as one community
solution: The spread of 'print' (the printing press, books, newspapers) and a common written or standardised language is said (notably by Benedict Anderson) to have played an important role in creating nations, because it enabled large numbers of people — most of whom would never meet one another — to share a common language, to read the same books, newspapers, and ideas, and thereby to develop a shared consciousness, a common frame of reference, and a sense of belonging to the same community. Through 'print capitalism' and a shared print-language, people spread across a wide territory came to imagine themselves as members of a single community (a nation) — reading the same news and ideas, sharing a common language and consciousness. In this way, print and a common language helped to create the shared consciousness and imagined community that constitute a nation, contributing to the rise of nations and nationalism in the modern era.

stem: National symbols such as the national flag and national anthem are important because they:
options: Serve as shared symbols of national identity, unity, and belonging, evoking a sense of common membership and attachment among the members of a nation
solution: National symbols — such as the national flag, the national anthem, national emblems, and other symbols — are important because they serve as shared, visible, and emotionally powerful symbols of national identity, unity, and belonging. They represent the nation and evoke among its members a sense of common membership, shared identity, attachment, pride, and solidarity — helping to give concrete and emotionally resonant expression to the shared identity and belonging that constitute the nation, and to foster a sense of common membership and unity among the diverse members of the nation. National symbols thus play an important role in expressing, reinforcing, and evoking national identity, unity, and belonging, and in giving tangible and emotionally powerful form to the 'imagined community' of the nation.

stem: The unification of Italy and Germany in the nineteenth century are historical examples of:
options: Nationalism as a force for uniting many separate states or regions into a single nation-state
solution: The unification of Italy and of Germany in the nineteenth century are historical examples of nationalism acting as a force for uniting many separate, previously independent or fragmented states, principalities, or regions into a single, larger nation-state. In both cases, nationalist movements and sentiments — the sense that the people shared a common national identity and should be united in a single nation-state — drove the process of bringing together the many separate states into a unified Italian and German nation-state respectively. These are classic examples of the unifying face of nationalism — its power to bring together separate states and regions, on the basis of a shared national identity, into a single nation-state — which was an important force in nineteenth-century Europe. (Nationalism can thus act both to unite separate units into one nation-state, as in Italy and Germany, and, conversely, to break up larger states, as in movements for national independence or secession.)

stem: The 'two-nation theory' that led to the partition of British India in 1947 held that:
options: Indians of all religions formed a single nation
Hindus and Muslims constituted two separate nations, and therefore Muslims should have a separate state (Pakistan)
Region, not religion, defined the nation
solution: The 'two-nation theory' that led to the partition of British India in 1947 held that Hindus and Muslims constituted two separate and distinct nations — defined by religion — with separate identities, interests, and ways of life, and that therefore the Muslims of India should have a separate nation-state of their own (Pakistan), distinct from a Hindu-majority India. This theory, based on a religious (ethnic/communal) conception of the nation, was advanced by the Muslim League as the basis for the demand for Pakistan, and it led to the partition of British India into two separate states (India and Pakistan) at independence in 1947 — a partition accompanied by mass migration, communal violence, and enormous human suffering. The two-nation theory (and the partition it produced) is a significant and tragic example of a religious/communal conception of nationhood, and it stands in contrast to the inclusive, composite, and civic conception of Indian nationalism championed by the Indian national movement, which held that Indians of all religions and communities formed a single, inclusive nation. The two-nation theory and the partition of India illustrate the profound consequences — including division, violence, and suffering — that can flow from a narrow, religious, or communal conception of the nation.

stem: A 'plebiscite' or referendum, in the context of self-determination, is:
options: A direct vote by the people of a territory to decide their political future or status (e.g., whether to join a state or become independent)
solution: A 'plebiscite' (or referendum) is a direct vote by the people of a territory or region to decide an important political question about their status or future — for example, whether the territory should become independent, join one state or another, or accept a particular political arrangement. In the context of the principle of self-determination, a plebiscite is often seen as a democratic means of ascertaining and giving effect to the will of the people of a territory regarding their political future — allowing them to determine, by their own vote, their political status and destiny. Plebiscites reflect the democratic principle that the people themselves should decide their political future, and they have been used (or demanded) in various disputes over territory and self-determination. However, plebiscites can also be difficult and contentious — for example, over who is entitled to vote, how the question is framed, and how to deal with mixed populations and minorities — and the demand for or holding of a plebiscite is often bound up with difficult political disputes and conflicts over self-determination and the status of territories.

stem: The composite culture of India (the mixing and blending of diverse cultural traditions over centuries) supports which conception of Indian nationhood?
options: An inclusive, pluralistic, and composite nationhood, in which the nation is enriched by and embraces its diverse cultural traditions
A nationhood based on one language only
solution: The composite culture of India — the mixing, blending, and mutual enrichment of diverse cultural, religious, and regional traditions over many centuries — supports an inclusive, pluralistic, and composite conception of Indian nationhood, in which the nation is understood to be enriched by, and to embrace, its diverse cultural traditions, rather than being defined by a single religion, language, or culture. On this view, Indian civilisation and culture have been shaped by the coming together and blending of many diverse influences and traditions (across religions, regions, and communities), producing a rich, composite, and pluralistic culture; and Indian nationhood is understood as inclusive and composite — embracing and drawing strength from this diversity, rather than seeking to impose a single uniform identity. This composite and pluralistic conception of Indian nationhood — 'unity in diversity' — stands in contrast to narrow, exclusive, or single-religion conceptions of the nation (like the two-nation theory), and it reflects the inclusive, civic, and pluralistic form of nationalism championed by the Indian national movement and embodied in the Indian Constitution, which seeks to unite India's diverse peoples in a shared, inclusive nationhood that respects and embraces their diversity.

stem: The principle of self-determination, when applied to national minorities within existing states, poses the dilemma of:
options: How to respect the aspirations of minorities for autonomy or recognition without necessarily fragmenting existing states, since not every group can have its own state
Always granting every group a separate state
solution: The principle of self-determination, when applied to national minorities within existing states, poses a difficult dilemma: how to respect and accommodate the aspirations of minority national groups for autonomy, recognition, and self-government, without necessarily fragmenting existing states or leading to endless division and conflict — given that not every group claiming to be a nation can realistically have its own separate state. On the one hand, the principle of self-determination suggests that national groups should be able to determine their own political future and govern themselves. On the other hand, since populations are mixed and there are far more national groups than could be given separate states, granting every group its own state is neither possible nor desirable (and could lead to endless fragmentation, conflict, and new minorities). The dilemma is thus how to honour the legitimate aspirations of national minorities — for the recognition and protection of their identity, and for a degree of autonomy and self-government — through means (such as federalism, autonomy arrangements, and minority rights) that accommodate these aspirations within existing states, rather than requiring the fragmentation of states into ever-smaller units. Finding ways to accommodate the aspirations of national minorities for autonomy and recognition within existing states — reconciling the claims of self-determination with the maintenance of the unity and integrity of states and the peaceful coexistence of diverse groups — is one of the central and difficult challenges posed by the principle of self-determination and by the reality of national diversity within states.

stem: Federalism can be a means of accommodating national and regional diversity because it:
options: Concentrates all power at the centre
Allows different regions or groups a degree of self-government and autonomy within a single state, giving them a stake and a sense of belonging while maintaining overall unity
solution: Federalism can be an important means of accommodating national, regional, and linguistic diversity within a single state, because it allows different regions or groups a degree of self-government, autonomy, and control over their own affairs (within their own sphere), while maintaining the overall unity and integrity of the state. By granting regions or groups their own governments and a share of power and autonomy, federalism gives them a stake in the political system, a means of protecting and expressing their distinct identities and interests, and a sense of belonging and self-government within the larger nation — thereby helping to reconcile the accommodation of diversity with the maintenance of national unity. Federalism thus offers a way of honouring the aspirations of regional and national groups for self-government and recognition, and of accommodating diversity, without fragmenting the state — allowing a diverse society to hold together as a single nation while granting its constituent regions and groups a degree of autonomy and self-government. India's federal structure (with states, many organised on linguistic lines) is an important example of the use of federalism to accommodate the country's vast linguistic, regional, and cultural diversity within a single, united nation — helping to reconcile unity with diversity and to hold together a highly diverse country. Federalism is thus one of the important institutional means by which diverse societies can accommodate their diversity and the aspirations of their regional and national groups within a single, united state, reconciling the accommodation of diversity with the maintenance of national unity.

stem: The claim that 'nations are not eternal, and neither did they always exist' points to the fact that:
options: Nations came into being at particular times in history and are the product of specific historical processes and circumstances, rather than being timeless, natural entities
Nations are purely imaginary with no reality
solution: The claim that 'nations are not eternal, and neither did they always exist' points to the important fact that nations are not timeless, eternal, or purely natural entities, but came into being at particular times in history and are the product of specific historical processes, developments, and circumstances. Although nationalists often present their nations as ancient, timeless, or natural, historical and scholarly study suggests that nations (and nationalism) are, to a significant extent, modern phenomena — that they emerged and were formed under particular historical conditions and through particular processes (as the modernist view of nationalism emphasises). This does not mean that nations are unreal or unimportant — they are very real and powerful in their effects — but it means that they are historically formed and constructed, rather than being eternal, natural givens; they have histories, they came into being at particular times, and they can and do change over time. Recognising the historically formed and constructed (rather than eternal or natural) character of nations is an important insight for understanding nationalism, and it cautions against the nationalist tendency to present nations as timeless, natural, or unchanging, reminding us instead that nations are historically formed communities, shaped by particular historical processes and circumstances, and capable of change and development over time.

stem: The relationship between the idea of the nation and the idea of popular sovereignty (the people as the source of authority) is that:
options: The rise of nationalism was closely connected to the idea that sovereignty belongs to the nation/people, who should govern themselves — linking nationhood to democratic self-rule
Only kings have sovereignty in a nation
solution: The relationship between the idea of the nation and the idea of popular sovereignty (the principle that ultimate authority and sovereignty belong to the people) is close and historically connected. The rise of modern nationalism was closely bound up with the emergence of the idea of popular sovereignty — the idea that sovereignty and ultimate authority belong not to a king or ruler but to the nation, understood as the people, who should therefore govern themselves. In this connection (associated especially with the French Revolution), the nation (the people) was seen as the source of political authority and the proper bearer of sovereignty, and nationalism was linked to the demand that the nation/people should be free from arbitrary rule and should govern itself — connecting nationhood to democratic self-rule and self-determination. In this sense, the idea of the nation and the idea of popular sovereignty and democratic self-government grew up together and reinforced each other: the nation was conceived as a community of people entitled to sovereignty and self-government, and nationalism was connected to the democratic ideas of popular sovereignty and self-rule. This historical connection between nationalism and popular sovereignty/democratic self-government is an important aspect of the relationship between nationalism and democracy, and it helps explain why nationalism and democracy often went together historically (both asserting that the nation/people should be sovereign and should govern themselves), even though, as noted, nationalism can also take undemocratic forms. The link between the nation, popular sovereignty, and self-government is thus an important part of the modern idea of the nation and of nationalism.

stem: One reason it is difficult to define a 'nation' precisely is that:
options: Different nations are based on different combinations of factors (history, territory, language, culture, shared political ideals), and no single factor is common to, or essential for, all nations
Nations have no basis at all
solution: One reason it is difficult to define a 'nation' precisely is that different nations are formed and held together on the basis of different combinations of factors — such as shared history and memories, attachment to a common territory or homeland, a common language or culture, common ethnicity or religion, and shared political ideals and aspirations — and no single one of these factors is common to, or essential for, all nations. Some nations are held together primarily by a shared language or culture, others by a common history and territory, others by shared political ideals and institutions (as in civic nations), and so on; and many nations are based on a mixture of these factors. Because there is no single, uniform basis or defining characteristic common to all nations — because nations are formed on different and varied bases — it is difficult to give a single, precise, and universally applicable definition of what a nation is. This diversity in the bases of nationhood is one of the reasons why the concept of the nation is complex and difficult to define precisely, and why definitions of the nation tend to emphasise the shared sense of collective identity, belonging, and common political aspiration among the members (which is common to nations) rather than any single 'objective' factor (like language or territory) that all nations share. The difficulty of defining the nation precisely reflects the varied and complex bases on which different nations are formed and held together.

stem: Mahatma Gandhi's conception of Indian nationalism emphasised:
options: An inclusive nationalism based on non-violence, the unity of all Indians (across religions and communities), and moral and humane values, rather than narrow hatred or exclusiveness
solution: Mahatma Gandhi's conception of Indian nationalism emphasised an inclusive, humane, and moral nationalism — based on non-violence (ahimsa), the unity and brotherhood of all Indians across religions, communities, and regions, and moral and humane values — rather than narrow hatred, exclusiveness, or aggression. Gandhi sought to unite all Indians — Hindus, Muslims, and people of all religions and communities — in a shared, inclusive struggle for freedom and a common, composite nationhood, and he emphasised communal harmony, the unity of all Indians, and moral and spiritual values. His nationalism was directed against the injustice of colonial rule and for the freedom and upliftment of India, but it was not based on hatred of the British people or on narrow religious or communal exclusiveness; rather, it sought to unite all Indians in an inclusive nationhood grounded in non-violence, communal harmony, and moral and humane values, and it even sought to win over opponents through non-violence and moral appeal rather than hatred and violence. Gandhi's inclusive, non-violent, and humane conception of nationalism — emphasising the unity of all Indians, communal harmony, non-violence, and moral values — represents an important and distinctive form of nationalism, and it contributed to the inclusive, composite, and pluralistic character of Indian nationalism at its best, in contrast to narrow, exclusive, or aggressive forms of nationalism.

stem: The 'nation-building' process in newly independent countries involves:
options: The often long and challenging task of forging a sense of common national identity, unity, and shared institutions among diverse groups, and building a viable state
The breaking up of the country
solution: The 'nation-building' process, especially in newly independent countries (such as those that emerged from colonial rule), involves the often long, difficult, and challenging task of forging and strengthening a sense of common national identity, unity, and solidarity among the country's diverse groups and communities, and of building viable and effective state institutions and a shared political community. Newly independent countries often inherited populations that were highly diverse (in religion, language, ethnicity, region, and culture), and that did not always have a strong or well-established sense of common national identity or shared institutions; the task of nation-building was to forge, among these diverse peoples, a sense of common nationhood, unity, and belonging, and to build the shared institutions, values, and identity of a viable nation-state — a task that was often long, difficult, and challenging, and that involved managing and accommodating diversity, overcoming divisions, and creating a sense of shared identity and common purpose. India's own experience since independence — of building a sense of common Indian nationhood, unity, and shared democratic institutions among its enormously diverse population, while accommodating and respecting that diversity — is an important example of the challenging process of nation-building. The nation-building process highlights that national unity and identity are not always simply given, but often have to be actively forged, built, and strengthened over time, especially in diverse and newly independent countries — an ongoing and challenging task that is central to the consolidation and success of new nation-states.

stem: The idea that a nation should have the right to self-determination gained international recognition especially:
options: In the twentieth century, notably after the World Wars and during decolonisation, when it inspired and legitimised the independence of many colonised peoples
solution: The idea that a nation (or people) should have the right to self-determination gained wide international recognition and prominence especially in the twentieth century — notably after the First and Second World Wars and during the period of decolonisation — when it inspired, legitimised, and provided a powerful basis for the independence of many colonised peoples and the emergence of numerous new independent nation-states from the former colonial empires. The principle of self-determination — that peoples have the right to determine their own political status and to govern themselves, free from foreign domination — became an important and widely recognised principle in international politics and law, championed by nationalist and anti-colonial movements, and it played a central role in the great wave of decolonisation that led to the independence of many countries (including India) in the twentieth century. The international recognition and influence of the principle of self-determination in the twentieth century — as a basis for the freedom and independence of colonised and dominated peoples — was thus a significant development, and it reflected and reinforced the power of nationalism and the aspiration of peoples for freedom and self-government. At the same time, as noted, the principle of self-determination also raised difficult questions and challenges (about which groups are entitled to it, and about the problems of applying it to national minorities within states and to mixed populations), which have continued to be important and contentious issues in international politics.

stem: The relationship between respecting diversity and maintaining national unity, as India's experience shows, is that:
options: It is possible to combine national unity with the respect and accommodation of diversity — 'unity in diversity' — through inclusive nationhood, federalism, minority rights, and democratic accommodation
Unity requires the elimination of all diversity
Diversity and unity have no relationship
solution: The relationship between respecting diversity and maintaining national unity, as India's experience powerfully shows, is that it is possible — though challenging — to combine national unity with the respect and accommodation of diversity, an ideal often expressed as 'unity in diversity'. India, one of the most diverse countries in the world, has sought to build and maintain national unity not by suppressing or eliminating its enormous religious, linguistic, cultural, and regional diversity, but by respecting, accommodating, and even celebrating that diversity — through an inclusive and composite conception of Indian nationhood (that embraces all its diverse peoples), a federal structure (that grants regions and linguistic groups a degree of self-government and recognition), guarantees of minority rights and secularism (that protect the identities and rights of diverse religious and cultural groups), and democratic institutions and processes (that allow for the peaceful accommodation and negotiation of diversity and difference). India's experience suggests that national unity and the respect and accommodation of diversity, far from being necessarily opposed, can be combined and made mutually supporting — that a diverse society can be held together as a united nation precisely by respecting and accommodating its diversity, rather than by suppressing it. This ideal of 'unity in diversity' — of building and maintaining national unity through the respect and accommodation of diversity, rather than through its suppression or the imposition of uniformity — is a central and distinctive feature of the Indian approach to nationhood, and it offers an important example and lesson for the challenge, faced by many diverse societies, of reconciling national unity with the accommodation of diversity. It represents the inclusive, pluralistic, and accommodative form of nationalism, in contrast to the narrow, exclusive, and uniformity-imposing forms that suppress diversity in the name of unity, and it shows that the accommodation of diversity can be a source of strength and a means of achieving genuine and durable national unity, rather than a threat to it.

stem: A key insight about nationalism is that it can serve as a force for both liberation and oppression, meaning that:
options: The same force that liberates a people from foreign domination can, in a different form, be used to oppress minorities or attack other nations — so its moral value depends on the form it takes
solution: A key insight about nationalism is that it can serve as a force for both liberation and oppression — that the same powerful force which can liberate a people from foreign domination and injustice (as in the anti-colonial national liberation movements) can, in a different form, be used to oppress minorities, suppress dissent, or attack and dominate other nations (as in aggressive, exclusive, or chauvinistic nationalism). Nationalism, in other words, is a double-edged force, capable of both good and evil, of both liberation and oppression, depending on the form it takes and the ends to which it is directed. In its inclusive, tolerant, and liberating form, nationalism can unite people, inspire freedom struggles, and foster solidarity and self-government; in its narrow, aggressive, exclusive, or chauvinistic form, it can breed hatred, aggression, oppression, and conflict, and can be used to persecute minorities and attack other nations. The moral value of nationalism thus depends crucially on the form it takes — on whether it is inclusive, tolerant, and humane, or narrow, aggressive, and exclusive. This insight — that nationalism can be a force for both liberation and oppression, and that its moral value depends on its form — is important for understanding the complex and ambivalent character of nationalism, and it underlines the importance of cultivating the inclusive, tolerant, and humane forms of nationalism (which unite people and inspire freedom and solidarity) while guarding against the narrow, aggressive, and exclusive forms (which breed hatred, oppression, and conflict). It reminds us that nationalism is neither simply good nor simply bad, but a powerful force whose effects depend on how it is understood, directed, and expressed — and that the challenge is to harness its positive, liberating, and unifying potential while avoiding its negative, oppressive, and destructive potential.

stem: The chapter suggests that, given the reality of diverse states and the problems of self-determination, a reasonable approach is to:
options: Grant every group its own state
Protect the rights and identities of minorities and accommodate diversity within existing states (through rights, autonomy, and democratic means), rather than endlessly redrawing borders
solution: The chapter suggests that, given the reality that almost all states are diverse and contain minorities, and given the serious problems and dangers of trying to apply the principle of self-determination by granting every group its own separate state (which could lead to endless fragmentation, conflict, and new minorities), a reasonable and preferable approach is to protect the rights and identities of minorities and to accommodate diversity within existing states — through the recognition and protection of minority rights, arrangements for autonomy and self-government (such as federalism), and democratic means of accommodating and negotiating diversity and difference — rather than endlessly redrawing borders and fragmenting states in the pursuit of homogeneous nation-states. On this view, the goal should be to make existing, diverse states more just, inclusive, and accommodating of their diversity — protecting the rights, identities, and legitimate aspirations of minorities and diverse groups, and giving them a fair place, a sense of belonging, and a degree of self-government within the existing state — rather than to seek to create a separate state for every group (which is neither possible nor desirable, and which could lead to great conflict and instability). This approach seeks to reconcile the accommodation of diversity and the legitimate aspirations of minorities with the maintenance of the unity and integrity of states and the peaceful coexistence of diverse groups, by accommodating diversity within existing states through rights, autonomy, and democratic means. It reflects the recognition that, in a world of diverse states, the just and peaceful accommodation of diversity — the protection of minority rights and identities, and the granting of a fair place and appropriate autonomy to diverse groups within existing states — is generally a better and more workable approach than the endless fragmentation of states in pursuit of the unrealisable ideal of homogeneous nation-states. This is an important practical conclusion about how to deal with the challenges posed by national diversity and the principle of self-determination in the real world of diverse states.

stem: The claim that shared political ideals and aspirations can bind a nation together suggests a 'civic' conception of the nation, in which:
options: Membership is based only on ethnicity or religion
The nation is defined by a shared commitment to common political values and institutions, so that people of different backgrounds can belong to it
Only one ethnic group can belong
The nation has no shared values
solution: The claim that shared political ideals and aspirations can bind a nation together reflects a 'civic' conception of the nation, in which the nation is defined not by a common ethnicity, religion, or descent, but by a shared commitment to common political values, ideals, and institutions (such as democracy, equality, liberty, and a shared constitution). In this civic conception, people of diverse ethnic, religious, and cultural backgrounds can all belong to and be equal members of the nation, so long as they share its political values and aspirations. This civic conception is more inclusive than an 'ethnic' conception (which defines the nation by common ancestry, ethnicity, or religion, and tends to exclude those who do not share these), and it is well suited to diverse societies like India, where the nation is held together by shared political ideals and aspirations rather than by a single ethnicity or religion.

stem: The difference between an 'ethnic' and a 'civic' conception of the nation is that the ethnic conception defines the nation by:
options: Common descent, ethnicity, language, or religion, whereas the civic conception defines it by shared political values and institutions open to all
solution: The difference between an 'ethnic' and a 'civic' conception of the nation lies in how the nation and its membership are defined. The ethnic conception defines the nation by common descent, ethnicity, language, culture, or religion — membership of the nation is a matter of belonging to a particular ethnic, linguistic, or religious group, and tends to be based on birth and ancestry, excluding those who do not share these characteristics. The civic conception, by contrast, defines the nation by a shared commitment to common political values, ideals, and institutions (like democracy, equality, and a shared constitution), so that membership is open to all who share these political values and aspirations, regardless of their ethnic, linguistic, or religious background. The civic conception is more inclusive and is better suited to diverse, multicultural societies, while the ethnic conception, though it can foster strong solidarity, tends to be exclusive and can lead to the marginalisation or exclusion of those who do not belong to the dominant ethnic or religious group.

stem: Which of the following is an example of the destructive potential of aggressive nationalism in the twentieth century?
options: The extreme nationalism and racism of Nazi Germany, which led to aggression, war, and the persecution and genocide of minorities
The founding of the United Nations
solution: A stark example of the destructive potential of aggressive and exclusive nationalism in the twentieth century is the extreme nationalism and racism of Nazi Germany, which was based on a narrow, aggressive, and racist conception of the nation, and which led to militaristic aggression, the Second World War, and the horrific persecution and genocide of minorities (most notably the Holocaust — the mass murder of millions of Jews and others). This tragic example illustrates the terrible dangers of narrow, aggressive, exclusive, and racist forms of nationalism — how nationalism, when it becomes chauvinistic, intolerant, and aggressive, can lead to war, oppression, persecution, and even genocide. It stands as a powerful warning of the destructive potential of the negative face of nationalism, and of the importance of cultivating inclusive, tolerant, and humane forms of national identity instead.

stem: The tension between nationalism and internationalism concerns:
options: How to reconcile loyalty and attachment to one's own nation with cooperation, peace, and a sense of shared humanity and responsibility among all nations and peoples
solution: The tension between nationalism and internationalism concerns how to reconcile loyalty, attachment, and pride in one's own nation with cooperation, peace, mutual respect, and a sense of shared humanity and responsibility among all nations and peoples. Nationalism emphasises attachment and loyalty to one's own nation, which can foster unity and solidarity but can also, in its narrow forms, breed hostility and conflict between nations. Internationalism, by contrast, emphasises cooperation, peace, solidarity, and a sense of shared humanity and common interest among all nations and peoples, transcending narrow national rivalries. The challenge is to combine a healthy, inclusive love of and attachment to one's own nation with respect for other nations, international cooperation, and a sense of shared humanity — to be a good patriot and also a good citizen of the world. This tension between national attachment and international cooperation and shared humanity is an important issue, especially in an interconnected world facing many global challenges that require cooperation among nations.

stem: The idea that a nation is an 'imagined community' is associated with the scholar:
solution: Benedict Anderson described the nation as an 'imagined community', because its members feel a bond of belonging even though most of them will never meet or know one another personally.

stem: The French thinker who argued that a nation is created by a shared past and the will to live together (a 'daily plebiscite') was:
solution: Ernest Renan, in his lecture 'What is a Nation?', argued that a nation is formed by a shared heritage of memories and sacrifices and the present-day desire to live together, which he called a 'daily plebiscite'.

stem: The great Indian poet who was critical of narrow and aggressive nationalism was:
solution: Rabindranath Tagore was critical of narrow, aggressive and exclusive nationalism; he warned against making the nation into an idol and stressed universal humanism over blind nationalism.

stem: 'Patriotism' is sometimes distinguished from 'nationalism' in that patriotism is:
options: Love of and devotion to one's country, without necessarily asserting superiority over others
solution: Patriotism is generally understood as love and devotion to one's own country and people, whereas aggressive nationalism can involve asserting the superiority of one's nation and hostility towards other nations.

stem: The 'two-nation theory' that led to the partition of British India held that:
options: Hindus and Muslims constituted two separate nations
There should be many small nations
solution: The 'two-nation theory', advanced by the Muslim League, held that Hindus and Muslims were two distinct nations and could not live together in one state, which led to the partition of British India in 1947 and the creation of Pakistan.

stem: Assertion (A): The principle of self-determination can create problems. Reason (R): Almost every state contains minorities, so redrawing borders for each group could lead to endless division and conflict.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Self-determination is problematic because nearly every state is internally diverse, so granting every group its own state could lead to endless fragmentation, new minorities and continued conflict — R explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): Nationalism has both positive and negative faces. Reason (R): It can unite people for freedom and democracy, but can also fuel hatred, exclusion and violence.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Nationalism has a positive face (uniting people, inspiring struggles for freedom and democracy) and a negative face (breeding hatred, intolerance and violence against 'outsiders' or minorities) — R explains A.

stem: The idea that nations are 'modern' constructions rather than eternal is supported by the fact that:
options: Nations and nationalism largely emerged in the modern era, aided by print and mass communication
solution: Historians argue that nations are relatively modern constructions; nationalism as a mass phenomenon emerged in the modern era, fostered by developments like print, a common language, education and mass communication.

stem: The spread of 'print' and a common written language is significant for nationalism because it:
options: Helped create a shared identity and sense of community among people
solution: The spread of print and a common written language allowed people across a territory to share ideas, news and a common culture, helping to create the shared identity and imagined community that underlies nationalism.

stem: The distinction between an 'ethnic' and a 'civic' conception of the nation is that:
options: An ethnic nation is based on shared descent/culture, while a civic nation is based on shared political values and citizenship
Civic nations are based on blood
solution: An ethnic conception defines the nation by common descent, language, religion or culture, whereas a civic conception defines it by shared political values, institutions and equal citizenship open to all, regardless of ethnicity.

stem: The composite culture of India (the blending of many cultures over centuries) supports the idea that:
options: Indian nationhood is inclusive and based on unity in diversity
solution: India's composite culture, formed by the mingling of many religions, languages and traditions over centuries, supports an inclusive conception of Indian nationhood based on unity in diversity rather than a single ethnic identity.

stem: Nationalism became a powerful force in the modern world especially from the:
options: Late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries (e.g. French Revolution, unification of Italy and Germany)
solution: Nationalism became a major political force from the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, with events like the French Revolution and the unification of Italy and Germany, and later inspired anti-colonial movements.

stem: The principle of self-determination played a major role in the twentieth century in:
solution: The principle of self-determination inspired anti-colonial movements across Asia and Africa in the twentieth century, as peoples claimed the right to determine their own future and win independence from colonial rule.

stem: Match the concept with its meaning: (i) Patriotism (ii) Chauvinism (iii) Self-determination — (a) aggressive belief in national superiority (b) love of one's country (c) right of a people to decide their political status:
solution: Patriotism is love of one's country, chauvinism is an aggressive belief in national superiority, and self-determination is the right of a people to decide their own political status.

stem: Federalism can help accommodate national and regional diversity by:
options: Sharing power between the centre and regions, giving groups a degree of self-government
solution: Federalism can accommodate the diversity of national, regional and linguistic groups by sharing power between the central and regional governments, giving different groups a measure of self-government within a united country.

stem: The claim that 'nations are not eternal' means that:
options: Nations came into being at a certain point in history and may change or dissolve
solution: The claim that nations are not eternal means that nations, like other human institutions, came into being at particular points in history, have evolved over time, and could in principle change or cease to exist.

stem: National symbols such as the flag and national anthem are important because they:
options: Help foster a shared sense of identity and belonging
solution: National symbols like the flag, anthem and other emblems help create and express a shared sense of national identity and belonging, uniting people around common symbols of the nation.

stem: A shared 'common history' contributes to national identity because it:
options: Gives people a sense of common heritage, memories and belonging
solution: A shared common history — including collective memories, achievements and struggles — gives the members of a nation a sense of common heritage and belonging, strengthening their national identity.

stem: Attachment to a particular territory (a homeland) is important to nationalism because:
options: A shared homeland gives the nation a physical space and focus for belonging
solution: Attachment to a specific territory or homeland is central to nationalism because the shared land gives the nation a physical focus for its identity, memories and sense of belonging, and a space to govern itself.

stem: The existence of national, ethnic and religious minorities within states means that:
options: States must find ways to accommodate diversity and protect minority rights
solution: Because almost every state contains national, ethnic, linguistic or religious minorities, states face the challenge of accommodating this diversity fairly and protecting the rights and identities of minorities within a shared nationhood.

stem: A 'nation' differs from other social groups (like a tribe or family) in that a nation:
options: Is a large community with a shared identity and the aspiration to govern itself
solution: A nation is distinguished from smaller social groups by being a large community of people who share a sense of common identity and history and who aspire to political self-government, usually within their own state.

stem: The unification of Italy and Germany in the nineteenth century is an example of nationalism:
options: Bringing together separate states into a single nation-state
solution: The unification of Italy and Germany in the nineteenth century shows nationalism working to bring together previously separate states and peoples sharing a common identity into a single unified nation-state.

stem: Indian nationalism, as it developed during the freedom struggle, was:
options: Inclusive, drawing together diverse religions, languages and regions against colonial rule
solution: Indian nationalism during the freedom struggle developed as an inclusive movement that united people of diverse religions, languages, castes and regions in the common cause of ending colonial rule and building a free, plural nation.

stem: Which of the following is an example of the destructive face of nationalism?
options: Ethnic cleansing or genocide driven by aggressive nationalism
solution: Ethnic cleansing, genocide, and wars driven by aggressive and exclusive nationalism (as seen in various twentieth-century conflicts) are examples of the destructive face of nationalism when it turns intolerant and violent.

stem: The recognition and celebration of a nation's diversity, rather than suppressing it, reflects:
solution: Celebrating rather than suppressing a nation's diversity reflects an inclusive nationalism based on 'unity in diversity', which India has sought to embody, holding together many cultures within a shared nationhood.

stem: The claim that shared political ideals and aspirations can bind a nation together suggests a __________ conception of the nation.
solution: The idea that shared political values, ideals and aspirations — rather than common ethnicity — can bind a nation together reflects a civic conception of nationhood, which India's inclusive nationalism approximates.

stem: The Indian approach to accommodating its diversity within a common nationhood includes:
options: Federalism, secularism, and the recognition of linguistic and cultural rights
solution: India accommodates its vast diversity within a common nationhood through federalism, secularism, the recognition of many languages, and the protection of minority and cultural rights, embodying unity in diversity.

stem: The relationship between respecting diversity and maintaining national unity is that:
options: Genuine unity is strengthened, not weakened, by respecting diversity
solution: Respecting and accommodating diversity, rather than suppressing it, can actually strengthen national unity by giving all groups a sense of belonging and fair treatment, as India's experience of unity in diversity suggests.

stem: A key insight about nationalism is that it can serve as a force for both:
solution: A key insight is that nationalism is double-edged: it can be a force for liberation, uniting people against colonial or oppressive rule, but it can also become a force for oppression when it turns aggressive and intolerant towards minorities or other nations.

stem: The chapter suggests that, given the reality of diverse societies, the best approach is a nationalism that:
options: Is inclusive and respects the rights and identities of all groups
solution: Given that most societies are diverse, the chapter suggests that the best form of nationalism is an inclusive one that respects the rights, identities and cultures of all groups while fostering a shared sense of belonging and unity.

stem: The reason it is difficult to define a 'nation' precisely is that:
options: No single factor (language, religion, territory) is common to all nations
solution: It is hard to define a nation precisely because no single objective factor — such as common language, religion, race or territory — is shared by all nations; ultimately, a nation rests on a subjective sense of belonging and shared aspiration.

stem: The ideal of 'unity in diversity' means that a nation:
options: Can be united while embracing and respecting its internal differences
solution: The ideal of 'unity in diversity', central to Indian nationalism, means that a nation can achieve genuine unity and shared belonging while embracing, respecting and celebrating its internal diversity of religions, languages and cultures.

stem: A serious challenge posed by the principle of self-determination is that:
options: It can lead to endless demands for separate states and new minorities
solution: A serious challenge of self-determination is that, since almost every group contains further sub-groups and minorities, granting each a separate state could lead to endless fragmentation, new minorities and continued conflict, so it must be balanced with other principles.
